utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours. Good morning to counsel. Good morning to everybody. Yesterday, when I left off, I was talking about evidence -- I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was talking about evidence as concerns Mr. Beara's -- Mr. Beara's presence in Zepa. I won't repeat that, but I will put on the record, for the benefit of my colleagues and for the Trial Chamber, a transcript reference, which is the transcript page 14603, 22, through 14604, line 7. With respect to the Defence's assertion concerning forcible transfer, Mr. Beara's participation in that joint criminal enterprise, they assert that there is no proof of contemporaneous or even subsequent knowledge of the civilians, and that's at paragraphs 376 through 379 of the brief. The claim is that: "Mr. Beara was not in Potocari and not aware of the crimes committed in Potocari, including the transfer of the civilian population." That's at paragraph 401. First, it is clear in the evidence of this case that his subordinates were on the ground in Potocari. Mr. Popovic concedes that he was present there. He doesn't contest it. Momir Nikolic was also there, and they were in the thick of things. The Main Staff and Drina Corps command structures were also clearly involved. Now, to suggest that Beara had no awareness of the predicament of the population is, to say the least, untenable. To the contrary, the knowledge and awareness of events, including the crimes perpetrated there, can be reasonably inferred from the conduct of his professional subordinates. His knowledge of those events is also implicitly shown in his interactions with Mr. Celanovic, PW-161, Miroslav Deronjic, as well as Momir Nikolic. He knows about prisoners. He's got to know how they came to be in Bratunac. He's got to know that many of them were separated and the circumstances under which they were separated, and it's abundantly clear that he knows what will happen to them. He exercises specialist control over the security organs and subordinate commands, and he has to know what they're doing and why. The Rules of Service indicate, and this is at -- sorry, the exhibit number is P00407. It's paragraph 12: "Security organs report on their work to their immediate superior and the security organs of superior commands, units, institutions, or staffs in accordance with the provisions of these rules." There's no question that Mr. Beara knows about the predicament of the civilian population in respect of their transfer. I want also to refer the Trial Chamber to P00480, and this is an interview that he gave on 29 October 2002, and in that interview - it's on page 7 - he was asked whether or not he participated in the operation of the Serbian forces entering Srebrenica. And he responds that he was away, that he was on the Bihac front, but he returned when it was -- when it was over. And he says: "One day, when I was taking mail to General Mladic, I saw a large number of buses on the road leading from Bratunac to Zepa and Srebrenica. The vehicles were sent from all over Bosnia to transfer the Muslims to Tuzla via Kalesija, an UNPROFOR convoy was providing security." To suggest that Mr. Beara doesn't have any information contemporaneous or subsequent with respect to the civilian population and their forcible removal is, as I say, untenable. The Defence brief also asserts that there was no ethnic animus that was part of the character of Mr. Beara, and if he committed any of these crimes, it wasn't motivated, essentially, by that animus. I think you've seen the evidence of that animus at this trial. You've seen it evidenced in the intercepts by his persistent and continuous use of pejorative and derogatory remarks to describe the Muslims. You've seen it used in official documents that he's distributed to his subordinates and to his contemporaries. I won't go into all of those, because I think the record is replete with the evidence of that animus, and I would submit that it affected Mr. Beara's behaviour and it affected the motives with which he participated in the commission of the offences that are charged under the indictment. In the Prosecution's opening address, Mr. McCloskey referred to Mr. Beara as an empty vessel. At paragraph 493 of the Beara brief, the Beara Defence suggests that this means that he had no power or authority to influence the course of events. Even though Mr. Beara was not a commander, of course he had the power to influence the course of events, of course he did. Invested with the powers, the authority and under the orders of his commander, he clearly did. He influenced the course of events, and he significantly contributed to the -- significantly contributed to the JCEs that are charged in the indictment. Those events, as you know, and as is proved in this case, culminated in the murders of thousands of people and the genocide. There has been no evidence of remorse in this case from Mr. Beara. I think the evidence actually points to the contrary, and it's something that we would ask that you consider in determining the appropriate sentence, should you find him guilty of the charges that are contained in the indictment. Again, I will refer you to the interview that he gave on 29 October 2002. At page 7 of that interview, despite Mr. Beara's clear involvement in the crimes that are charged in this indictment, he states: "Everyone knew that the Muslims killed their own people in order to accuse the Serbs so that the NATO could launch air-strikes against us because of crimes against civilians. I am convinced that Markale is a mini Srebrenica and a mini Zepa." He then has the temerity to tell this reporter how the crimes and the murders of thousands could be committed if someone had such an idea to do it; that is to say, if it had actually even happened. With respect to that, he says -- the question to him is: "Are you trying to say that the VRS did not commit mass crimes in Srebrenica?" And his answer is: "They didn't. The Hague allegedly has a list of mass grave locations. They say there are 800 bodies in one mass grave, 2.000 in another, and 3.000 in yet another one. They claim they are primary and secondary graves, alleging we moved bodies. What nonsense. It is not possible to carry out killings on such a mass scale in the presence of UN representatives, even if someone had such an insane idea." Your Honours, the evidence in this case establishes Mr. Beara's involvement and clear responsibility for the crimes that are charged under the indictment, and we ask that you hold him responsible and you find him guilty. This concludes my submissions with respect to Mr. Beara. And if I may, I'd like to turn to Mr. Popovic. The evidence of Mr. Popovic's guilt and involvement in these horrendous crimes is clear and it is compelling. As I mentioned before, Your Honours, the Popovic brief challenges the very foundations of the indictment, and because it, like the Beara brief, is diametrically opposed to so many of the fundamental tenets of the Prosecution's case, many of the arguments raised in the Popovic closing brief are dealt with in the Prosecution's final brief. In particular, the Popovic brief challenges the credibility of several inculpatory witnesses, as it should. It challenges among them PW-128, PW-101, who they assert knowingly gave false testimony. The brief similarly attacks the testimony of Momir Nikolic and Miroslav Deronjic, as well as certain other significant inculpatory witnesses. The credibility of these witnesses are discussed in the Prosecution's final brief and I won't be addressing these. I will again try to confine my arguments to some of the more fundamental issues that respond to the Defence brief and also highlight Mr. Popovic's involvement in and contributions to the JCEs, as are pled in the indictment. Now, because the Defence has devoted a substantial amount of time to the viability of the intercept evidence in this case, I think a few points should be made in that regard, also because the Beara Defence similarly challenges that evidence. Now, you heard the evidence of 28 intercept operators in this case from the ABiH 2nd Corps, Anti-Electronic Warfare Department, the 21st Division, and also the ABiH MUP. You heard this over several months, including the testimony of platoon commanders, squad commanders, and supervisors. You received testimony on the process of interception, the mechanics of it, the notebooks, the print-outs, the physical equipment, the training of the operators and their technical backgrounds. You've also heard about the protocols and the standards that were in place and that they employed during the process of interception. You heard from the Prosecution witness or Prosecution analyst concerning the intercept project that was compiled in order to validate and authenticate the intercept evidence. You heard about the chain of custody, and you had an opportunity to consider all of these issues in determining the admissibility of this evidence in advance of the Defence case. I submit that all of these witnesses establish beyond question the accuracy, authenticity, and reliability of this evidence, and the witnesses that have been adduced by the Defence do not change this. You heard from Nedjo Blagojevic, the communications officer in the Drina Corps. He's the one who told you that interception was impossible. He also confirmed to you, though, that a failure to follow the rules would result in the type of intercept evidence that we have in this very case. That's at transcript 22333, 18 through 22. A report that was issued by Mr. Popovic also confirms the occurrence of sloppy practices in the use of communication equipment within the VRS ranks. That's Exhibit 3D00319. He states in that exhibit: "We have obtained information that our units are extremely -- extremely careless when using communications equipment." You've heard from Defence witness Velo Pajic, and he was -- he worked with the 67th Communication Regiment. He acknowledged that it was possible to intercept along radio relay routes. He's the one who, in giving an example about being able to change frequencies by moving up or down of a megahertz or two, came up with a number, 783, as an example, which happened to correspond within a frequency -- within a megahertz or two to some 95 of 148 possible RRU-800 intercepts that are in the evidence of this case. And, of course, you heard from Djuro Rodic, who was the principle Defence expert, who testified about the technical capabilities of the ABiH to intercept the VRS. I want to remind the Trial Chamber that Mr. Rodic conceded that the interception by the ABiH on both RRU-1 and RRU-800 radio relay devices was, in principle, possible. He stated at transcript 12513, lines 5 through 9. "Q. I think you indicated at the beginning of your testimony that generally it was possible for the ABiH to intercept communications? "A. Yes, this is what I stated with regard to the equipment that covered the frequency range of the RRU-1 and RRU-800. Under certain circumstances, it could intercept conversations." He then went on to talk about the circumstances or the reasons why they could not successfully intercept these communications. He reached his conclusions based upon calculations on the technical specifications of certain equipment that he reviewed, and he even suggested that one of the reasons they couldn't intercept VRS communications is because of an improper antenna orientation. In other words, he suggested they were pointing their antennas in the wrong direction. In light of the evidence in this case, it's clear that this suggestion is absurd. First, the radio relay networks in the former Yugoslavia were not a secret to any party to the conflict. It pre-existed that conflict, and they were known to everyone. Remember, there was a working map that was introduced into evidence in this case, P01468. It was an ABiH working map concerning radio relay communications. Mr. Rodic was confronted with this map and conceded that the map correctly depicted the radio relay devices on the route from Vlasenica through Zvornik, which has been contested by the Defence in this case. The map clearly indicates that they had the ability and certainly had the knowledge as to where to intercept and where to direct their antennas. In addition, there is evidence that the ABiH knew the frequencies that the Defence claimed never changed from 1993. That's evidenced in a document that's P02822, which reflects a working frequency which corresponded to the frequency plan that was issued in 1993 that was testified to by Mr. Blagojevic and testified to by Mr. Rodic. That frequency is 680 megahertz, and it corresponds to the route from Veliki Zep to Vlasenica on that claim. The conclusion for the Defence arguments can only be that although the ABiH could clearly identify frequencies on a working plan from 1993, that for some reason in 1995 they weren't able to identify that same frequency and they no longer knew where to point their antennas. In 1993, Drago Nikolic issued a report, and in his report, P03425, and it's dated 22 April 1993, in that report he stated: "We have confirmation that the enemy is intensively intercepting our radio and radio relay communications, and particularly active are their interception centres in Tuzla and in Gorazde." You can see how obviously absurd the Defence position is with respect to the capacity of the ABiH to intercept, and I'll leave it there, Your Honours. I'm confident that upon a review of all the credible evidence in this case, you will find that this evidence is accurate, you will find that it's highly reliable, and you will find it is extremely probative evidence of the circumstances in this case and, more importantly, of the acts and conduct of the accused. Now, in the case of Mr. Beara, the intercept evidence, in conjunction with other compelling documentary and testimonial evidence in this case, establishes -- just as it established in the case of Ljubisa Beara, it establishes the same hands-on involvement in the crimes that are charged in the indictment for Mr. Popovic, and it establishes his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. This evidence can't be reviewed or viewed in fragments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I recall, from reading, if I'm not mistaken, because I don't have it here with me, Popovic's final brief, if I remember well - that could be Beara, but I think it's Popovic - there is a submission that there is evidence that up to, if I remember well, 8th of August of 1995, the antenna of the ABiH for the purposes of intercepting the antenna were directed towards another region where there was conflict, too, in such a way that it, therefore, excluded the possibility of intercepting communication inside the Drina Corps area of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if it's Popovic or not. But what do you have to say about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the orientation of the antenna?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the conclusion, then, that that would have eliminated the possibility of intercepting communications by -- and to the Drina Corps inside the other area to which the antenna were not pointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I can answer the question, but I think I may have to go into private session to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, or if you prefer to leave it until later, when we come to the question stage, you can do that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: However you prefer, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. We can do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Initially, I wanted to respond to the assertion made by the Popovic Defence in its brief that there was no legal act putting the captured persons in the competence of the security organs, and that's at paragraph 675. I guess the suggestion here is that Mr. Popovic had no responsibility for involvement with the POWs in this case. Now, although this has been dealt with in the brief, I think it's important to point out -- point out that it is addressed in the testimony of Mr. Butler and it's addressed in his evidence, and in particular the command responsibility report. It also bears pointing out at the outset that the involvement of the Security Administration -- security organs in matters relating to prisoners is contemplated in relation to their control of the military police. That's clearly set out in the Rules, and Mr. Butler talked about that at transcript 19638, 1 through 19 -- and, I should say, 19940, 14 through 10. This has been illustrated in terms of the documents that have been produced in this case; that is, the relationship between the security organ and the military police and prisoners, in various documents. One of these documents is P00196, as an example of the interaction between the security organs and the subordinate security organs as well as concerns prisoners of war. And that document is signed by Mr. Popovic, and it passes on a Main Staff direction concerning the treatment of prisoners. It reads that: "All prisoners --" In part, I should say: "All prisoners, members of the enemy army, are to be handcuffed or their hands tied with anything available immediately after their capture. They are to be searched, and all items are to be seised, apart from their clothing and footwear." It goes on to say that: "An official record is to be compiled." It goes on and says that: "The location where POWs are collected must be such that the prisoners are fully secured, as well as the people from the security organ, from the intelligence organ, and from the military police organ that engages in the interrogation and guards POWs." The Defence acknowledges they must -- at paragraph 676 of their brief, that the commander of the unit is authorised to give any legal order to his subordinates in the security organs. They assert, however, that there is no evidence that either General Krstic, or General Zivanovic, or the superior commander issued any orders to Mr. Popovic regarding prisoners. Your Honours, the proof of those orders -- the evidence of those orders is implicit in the conduct of Mr. Popovic and his direct involvement with those prisoners and in the murders and detentions and forcible transfers that were committed in this case. Before I address some of the substantively charged crimes concerning Mr. Popovic, I would like to address some of the claims made in the Defence brief about Mr. Popovic's involvement in the uncharged crime committed in Bisina. The Popovic brief challenges the evidence of his involvement in the execution of those 39 Muslim men there. He asserts what might be described as a partial alibi defence. Now, paragraph 654 of the brief, the Defence argues that Popovic was not there during the executions, themselves, but only arrived there later during the burials of the 39 men that had been shot and executed there. They argue that he was elsewhere in Zvornik at the time the executions were committed and arrived at the time that the burials were underway. They introduced three statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the sake of the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, they introduce the statement of Miljenko Koljic, that's Mr. Popovic's brother-in-law I believe, they introduced the statement of Dragisa Cojic, which is his co-worker, and then the statement of Slavisa Vlacic. This is an individual who the Defence asserts Mr. Popovic was with that morning, 23rd July 1995. I would submit that you should reject the alibi for the fundamental reason that neither Mr. Popovic's brother-in-law, Miljenko Koljic, nor any other witness can actually exclude that Mr. Popovic was indeed at the execution site at the time that the killings were carried out, because no one has attested to the date of their purported encounter with him. Neither is there any precise date ascertainable from the proffered statements. Now, although the Prosecution dispute the veracity or sufficiency of this partial alibi defence, even if you accept it, the fact of Mr. Popovic's presence at all, that is to say, in any respect, at the scene of this uncontested mass execution is powerful evidence of pattern of conduct in this case. It shows that Mr. Popovic knew about the executions. It shows that he was fully aware of the commission of these crimes, which he was obligated to put a stop to as a member of the Officer Corps of the VRS, and particularly as one vested with the power to arrest. Exhibit P00028 are the Military Prosecutor's Office guide-lines for determining criteria for criminal prosecution. At paragraphs 2 and 3 on page 8 of that document, it reads -- I should rather read both: "If officers merely find out that units of the armed forces of the Army of Republika Srpska or their members have committed or are committing such acts and take no measures to prevent the consequences of the acts, themselves, and expose perpetrators to criminal prosecution, this, in itself, makes them answerable for those criminal offences. It follows from the above that officers in all units must accept the obligation to draft reports on all incidents which might be regarded as criminal offences, regardless of whether they have been committed by members of the Army of Republika Srpska or by members of the enemy side, and to report to the Command any information learned about previous incidents." I think I'll stop there, and you have it in evidence and can review it. What's important about this, though, is that these guide-lines were issued, I believe, in 1992. 1992. This is something that Mr. Popovic would necessarily have been aware of, and the fact that he didn't take the measures that are prescribed, indeed, required, according to this document, is consistent with his participation in the criminal activities that he was observing. It tells you about his intent with respect not only to his involvement at this particular execution, but it also tells you about his intent as established by his presence at larger executions that took place earlier in Zvornik. The evidence concerning Bisina shows the elements of the Drina Corps military police, over which Mr. Popovic has control ex officio, as well as the 10th Sabotage Detachment, were principally involved in carrying out the executions in Bisina. I will note that these same elements were involved in the crimes that were perpetrated at the Branjevo Military Farm on the 16th of July. You have the testimony of a member of that 10th Sabotage Detachment who testified also to the presence of Drina Corps military police that escorted his unit to the Branjevo Farm the morning that those executions took place. Further, there is evidence that Mr. Popovic had a relatively close relationship with the 10th Sabotage Detachment itself. There is testimony in the record which indicates that he used to come to the unit and would talk to the commander. That's at transcript 14013, lines 15 and 16. There is also other evidence concerning this relationship which is set out in the brief and I won't go into here. You had the opportunity to see and evaluate the testimony of PW-172 and PW-175, and both establish the direct involvement of Mr. Popovic at Bisina. PW-172 places Mr. Popovic at Bisina throughout the executions and the burial operation. You heard how he described his interaction with Mr. Popovic and what he said to him after the executions were completed. He says, at transcript 32573, lines 18, through 32574, line 9: "I mustered the strength as much as I could and I approached Vujadin Popovic and what I felt was either fear or pity. I don't know how to explain. I rolled the film in my head, the journey that I had taken and what had happened. I had never spoken to Vujadin Popovic before or ever since then. I never approached him in any way. There was no need for me to do that. However, as I had been listening to the stories of other soldiers who were talking about officers, they all had nicknames. I didn't know how they actually addressed them when they spoke to them directly, probably calling them by their rank, and I suppose that I would have done that as well. In essence, General Zivanovic was referred to as Zile in soldiers' conversations, Krstic was referred to as Krle. Mr. Vujadin Popovic had the nickname Pop. At that moment, I mustered the strength to approach him. Something snapped in my head, and I didn't approach him as an officer at that moment. I approached him and I told him, 'Pop, what has just happened?' And he never replied to me." This testimony leaves no doubt as to either Mr. Popovic's presence at or his hands-on involvement in coordinating, organising and directing the execution of the 39 men that were killed in that remote area. It is unclear why the Defence brief, at paragraph 658, states that PW-172: "... saw Popovic after the events and could only infer that he was there previously." On cross-examination and in response to counsel's questions -- Defence counsel's questions, this is at transcript 32958, 11 through 17, he was put the following questions: "Q. Could you please answer whether you were certain about what you were telling us? "A. I believe he was there. "Q. If you say 'I believe' or 'I think,' does this mean that you are not absolutely certain? Just let me be more precise. While the executions were taking place, while the executions were taking place. "A. He was there." There's nothing equivocal about that, there's nothing ambiguous about that. As you know, PW-172's presence at the site is confirmed by vehicle logs which demonstrate his trip there. That's Exhibit P04425. In addition, PW-175 transported the elements of the 10th Sabotage Detachment that formed the execution squad from Dragasevac that morning. His evidence is also supported by vehicle logs and reflects the fact that Mr. Popovic was involved. You can find this at transcript reference 32782, lines 10 through 12. Popovic's involvement in these crimes is further consistent with an intercept connecting him to one of the victims that was later identified in this case by DNA evidence emerging from that grave-site. Your Honours, the only thing that Mr. Popovic was doing in Bisina on 23 July 1995, as the most senior officer present there, was coordinating, organising, and carrying out orders that he would have received from his commands to execute these men. There is really no other explanation for his presence there, no other explanation. The evidence in this case shows that his knowledge, intent, and conduct were the same concerning the prisoners that were held in the schools in the Zvornik area; the Orahovac school, where he was present on 14 July, the Rocevic school, where he was present on 15 July, the Kula school, where he was present on 16 July. The nature and extent of Mr. Popovic's involvement in the Bisina executions virtually parallels the circumstances of his presence and participation in the crimes that were committed in Zvornik. And before I address some of the more compelling evidence of Mr. Popovic's involvement in those executions and his significant contributions to the murder JCE, I will address his involvement in the forcible transfer JCE. Mr. Popovic's involvement in the JCE to forcibly remove the populations of Srebrenica and Zepa is clear in the record of this case. Mr. Popovic was involved in a discussion with General Krstic just after the Hotel Fontana meeting in which the buses that were used to transfer the women and children from Potocari was discussed. General Krstic, as you know, was heavily involved in the mobilisation of the transportation and buses from the early morning of 12 July, well in advance of the Hotel Fontana meeting. The evidence shows that Mr. Popovic was engaged in a discussion with General Krstic which involved security issues for the buses, including the structure of their -- of the column. That you can find in transcript reference 14590, lines 2 through 5. Mr. Popovic's assignment of Momir Nikolic to assist in and coordinate and organise the separation of Muslim men in Potocari and the transfer of women and children also demonstrates his immediate involvement in that process. At paragraph 386 of the Defence brief, they assert: "There were no reasons why Popovic should have thought the evacuation was being carried out illegally." First, Your Honours, you have clear evidence in this case as to the nature of the forcible separations that were carried out, the brutality of those acts, and the acts that were perpetrated against the separated men. I won't repeat that evidence because that, as you can imagine and as you know, has been extensively addressed in the Prosecution's final brief. We know that Mr. Popovic was physically present in Potocari on the 12th and the 13th of July, and he had an opportunity to observe and to become aware of the rampant and serious abuses and crimes that were being and had been committed by VRS forces that were there. On 13 July, in particular, he was seen near the White House where we know that men were separated -- separated men were detained, they were physically abused, and even some were killed. You'll recall the testimony of DutchBat officer Major Rutten who saw Mr. Popovic there. He saw him speaking to Serb officers, and he saw them giving them directions, instructions. Now, Mr. Rutten was an experienced officer himself and observed that Mr. Popovic appeared to be in command and authority. In other words, he was a clear presence there. There is ample evidence of criminality and illegality in plain view in Potocari. Mr. Popovic had to have been informed of that, if not had seen it personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I don't have the final brief in front of me, but I take it when Mr. Popovic referred to, in his final brief, this forcible transfer of women and children, but you're now addressing the separated men?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am. The reason why is because the forcible transfer of the women and children was facilitated by the separation of the men, and also Mr. Popovic was involved in the security aspect of the transportation of the women and children, as I've indicated, as referenced in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you expand the meaning of "facilitated"? So with the men, then you are suggesting that would be more difficult, impossible, to transfer the women and children?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, sir. No, Your Honour. I'm not suggesting it would be impossible. What I'm suggesting is that it creates a situation of insecurity among the people that are being transferred. When you're separated from your loved one and you don't know what's going to happen to them, it makes it easier or it makes a person more complicit or docile in terms of moving them. It is easier to hold a person, for example, in detention when they don't know what's going to happen to their loved one, and it is easier also to keep a loved one away from a person when they don't know what's going to happen to them when they're held in detention. The consequences of your actions, when you don't know what the results are going to be, is what influenced and substantially contributed to the climate of fear that facilitated the forcible transfer of the women and the children in Potocari, and the separation of the men was an integral part of that fear, it's an integral part of that -- of the impetus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. In terms of the illegality of the forcible transfer, this is also underscored in an intercept, P01113. It's a 12 July intercept at 1250 hours, and it involves General Mladic, and it underscores what Mr. Popovic must have known. I will point out, frankly, it's not addressed to Mr. Popovic, but it is an intercept in which General Mladic says, when he's told that the buses are rolling in order to pick up people and transport them out, he says: "They've all capitulated, they've surrendered, and we'll evacuate them all, those who want to and those who don't want to." He then goes on to talk about the security issues concerning the movement and transportation of those -- of those buses. These are the very same security issues that a witness in this case overheard being discussed by General Krstic with Mr. Popovic. To the same extent that Mr. Popovic knew of the security issues relative to the transfer of the population on those buses, the structure, the clearing of the roads, the mines, et cetera, he must have known of the illegal plan, he must have known of the plan to send those who wanted to and those who didn't want to out. At 9.30 in the morning on 13 July, Mr. Popovic met with General Mladic and General Krstic, as well as Dragomir Vasic at the command of the Bratunac headquarters. The topic of discussion there was, indeed, the continued evacuation of the remaining civilian population from Srebrenica to Kladanj. That meeting is memorialised in the dispatch that was prepared by Dragomir Vasic, and it's P00886. Mr. Popovic's presence at that meeting is memorialised -- I should say -- documented, I should say, in Momir Nikolic's statement of facts at paragraph 8. I don't believe that the Popovic brief addresses the forcible transfer of the thousands of separated men from the column who were taken to Zvornik, where they were executed, but his involvement in the transfer of these men is amply established in the record of this case. On 13 July, Mr. Popovic calls Drago Nikolic to tell him that the prisoners detained in Bratunac were to be transferred to Zvornik, where they were to be killed. The following day, Mr. Popovic, Mr. Beara, and Mr. Nikolic meet at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters where, based on the events, they both proceeded and followed that meeting, indicates that they clearly coordinated and organised the transfer and detention of those prisoners. Following the meeting, Mr. Popovic led a column of thousands of prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik, where they were received by Mr. Nikolic, and they were distributed in the schools in the Zvornik area which had been and were being prepared to carry out their execution. You've heard the testimony of PW-138. The Defence argue at their brief at paragraph 489 that that witness just wanted to protect himself from the responsibility of leading the convoy by stating that he was travelling behind Popovic, who was in his Golf and leading the convoy. Now, it's unclear exactly how that strategy or that admission would accomplish this end, since in neither event PW-138 would have been admitting that he was participating. Now, he could simply denied his involvement altogether, but in fact it's his admission of his involvement that lends to the credibility of his evidence, and it's the detail of his evidence that bears the hallmarks of the truth. His testimony shows Mr. Popovic's hands-on style of involvement in the transfer of these witnesses, and it is compelling. If you recall, PW-138 testified how Mr. Popovic told him to meet him near a bus station in Bratunac on the morning of 14 July. He told PW-138 where to park an APC that he had asked him to use. He appeared in his blue Golf and directed PW-138 to move up. He came back and told him to move some more. He then told him to refuel the APC, if he needed to refuel it. He then came back, and after a column of buses that had assembled behind the APC, and Momir Nikolic testified that he estimated it was about one and a half kilometres long, PW-138 testified that he followed Mr. Popovic up to Orahovac and Mr. Popovic set the pace as he followed. The evidence -- I should say this evidence, rather, also ties Mr. Popovic obviously directly to the murder operation itself, and it underscores his essential and significant contribution to its implementation. It shows his coordination and organisation in the implementation of the orders of the VRS command structures, and together with Drago Nikolic and Ljubisa Beara and the Zvornik Brigade Command, its personnel and resources, it shows how this operation was coordinated. The clearest indication of Mr. Popovic's knowledge and his involvement in the murder operation is demonstrated, as I say, by his blunt statement to Momir Nikolic on 12th July that, All the balija have to be killed. Momir Nikolic's -- Momir Nikolic suggested potential detention sites and execution sites with Mr. Popovic, which he says were discussed. You then have the call to Drago Nikolic on the evening of the 13th. Paragraph 244 of Mr. Popovic's brief disputes the evidence that he called Drago Nikolic to inform him of the plan to transport the Muslim men held in Bratunac and the Zvornik area -- held in Bratunac to the Zvornik area in order to be killed, and the reason they give: "He would never have conveyed it through a telephone conversation because he had warned of discipline during radio communications in his capacity as a security officer." Now, Your Honours, judging from the sheer volume of the intercepted material in this case, including several significant ones concerning Mr. Popovic directly, this argument is completely vacuous. As imprudent as it may be, the evidence in this case shows Mr. Popovic on several intercepts. It even shows him on intercepts with Drago Nikolic. And while this call, in particular, would have been obviously a very sensitive one, it clearly does not preclude the fact -- it clearly does not preclude the fact that it occurred, that it would have been made. The Defence dispute the existence of any plan to kill the detained Muslims and boys before 14 July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes. THE ACCUSED BEARA: [Interpretation] I really apologise, but I do have to go out for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Security, please escort him. Shall we proceed, Colonel Beara, or -- I don't think -- Mr. Ostojic, he's not dealing with him at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think we can proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In their brief, paragraph 457, the Popovic Defence argues that if such a plan had existed, it would have been implemented immediately on 12-13 July. Now, clearly there is several reasons why this would not be the case as well. First, it took time to separate the large number of men in Potocari. It took time to round up the thousands of prisoners that continued to be captured through the 13th of July. There is little doubt that the VRS was not prepared for the large number of prisoners that they managed to capture over that period of time. And also the large number of prisoners that they had custody of by 13 July made it impossible to carry out their murders quietly and efficiently in Bratunac. International agencies were still operating in the area. Now, in the interview that I referred to before involving Mr. Beara, he states: "It was not possible to carry out the killings on such a mass scale in the presence of UN representatives." And that makes sense. There's truth to that, given his involvement in these crimes. The evidence shows that Mr. Popovic was present at Orahovac, he was in Rocevic, and he was at Kula. The Popovic brief, at paragraph 682, denies that -- states that: "They deny the prisoners in Orahovac were under the control of Mr. Popovic." And it's not clear whether this is in reference to a command function, control in a command sense, or it is in its colloquial meaning. In either event, the evidence establishes clearly that he was there. Aside from PW-138, whose testimony the Popovic Defence impugns directly, there is evidence from Tanacko Tanic which puts him there. In addition, there's evidence from Milorad Bircakovic that puts him there, and in addition to that there's the evidence of PW-101 who described an officer that was at the execution site, that matched Mr. Popovic's description. In respect of the evidence presented -- in respect of this evidence, that is, the evidence of PW-101, who said he saw someone matching Mr. Popovic's description, essentially, that evening, at their brief, at paragraph -- in their brief, I'm sorry, at paragraph 513, the Popovic Defence asserts that he was not in Zvornik on the evening of 14 July. And in respect of that, the Popovic Defence called Gordan Bjelanovic, and I'm sure that the Trial Chamber recalls his testimony because it was completely unreliable and it was completely contrived. Mr. Bjelanovic testified first of all as an alibi witness and stated that: "When it comes to dates --" I'm sorry: "When it comes to exact dates and times, it's difficult." You may recall that he testified that he did not leave Vlasenica until after the fall of Srebrenica. This was completely contradicted by a prior statement that he had given 9 March 2001 to Mr. Petrusic in connection with his defence of General Krstic. In that statement, he claimed that he was present in Srebrenica from 5 through 12 July. And when he was confronted with this contradiction, his explanation was barely intelligible. At paragraph 618 of the Popovic brief, the Defence assert that the testimony of the Zvornik Brigade 2nd Battalion Commander Srecko Acimovic is not credible. As the Prosecution has indicated, there were several witnesses in this case who, because of the nature and extent of their involvement in these events, tended to minimise their personal exposure. Srecko Acimovic was one of those witnesses. That, of course, does not mean that everything that he says was not true. Mr. Popovic's presence at the school cannot be explained away by some motive that could be attributed to Mr. Acimovic to set him up, to frame him. There's no evidence of that. Further, the fact of Mr. Popovic's presence at the Rocevic school is characteristic of his presence in Orahovac, it is also characteristic of his presence at the Kula school, and it is also characteristic of his presence at Bisina, all of which support Mr. Acimovic's testimony concerning his presence in Rocevic. He testified that he spoke to Mr. Popovic between 8.30 and 9.30 on 14 July, the day before Mr. Popovic came to the school. He spoke to him at the Brigade Command headquarters. Now, given the contrived alibi defence of Goran -- I think it's Gordan Bjelanovic, it is entirely plausible that Mr. Popovic would have been at the school. There were executions that were being carried out in Petkovci on the 14th of July. There were executions being carried out in Orahovac on that day. Mr. Nikolic was in that area, Mr. Beara was in that area. It makes sense that Mr. Popovic was in that area, and it makes sense that he would have been at Rocevic on the 14th -- on the 15th, having been in Orahovac on the 14th and having been at Kula on the 16th. He was an integral part of this murder operation, and together with Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Beara, that's exactly what he was doing, he was implementing the murder operation. Now, with respect to his presence at Pilica, that's paragraph 683 of the Defence brief, the Defence denies that Popovic was at the Kula school at around noon on the 16th of July. The Defence concede, however, and I quote this, that: "It is possible that there was a person fitting his description there because there were many men fitting the description of Popovic, and also many men with mustaches have been seen on many videos and photos during this trial." Now, I've already gone over some of the reasons why Slavko Peric's identification of Mr. Beara and Mr. Popovic is reliable, but you will recall also that with respect to Mr. Popovic, Mr. Peric testified that he observed someone refer to him as "Pop." And we know from the intercept evidence in this case and the testimonial evidence in this case that this was Mr. Popovic's nickname. PW-172 testified to that also. Now, all the Defence have argued that a subordinate would not refer to Mr. Popovic as "Pop." PW-172's testimony actually speaks to the contrary. In addition to that, there is several instances in which you can see that officers that are junior to Mr. Popovic refer to him as "Pop" in the intercept evidence, among them Drago Nikolic. The Defence's concession that it is possible that somebody fitting this description -- fitting the description of Mr. Popovic was in and around Pilica on 16 July at noon, or somebody with a moustache may have been there, of course, neglects the aspect of Mr. Peric's identification of Mr. Popovic as "Pop," that somebody referred to him as "Pop," so the question then is: While there may have been other men fitting Mr. Popovic's description running around with moustaches in the VRS, how many of them also went by the nickname "Pop," how many of them were actually called "Popovic"? How many of those would have been hanging around with somebody who just happened to look just like Ljubisa Beara? How many of those would have happened to have referenced -- been referenced in intercepts corresponding to the events in Pilica on the same day when they happened to have been seen there? And how many of those would have had their names appear on fuel receipts that were directed to Pilica? The evidence that Vujadin Popovic was present at the Kula school and involved in the executions there is supported by independent documentary evidence, and it is established in the case beyond a reasonable doubt. The corroboration of that involvement is found in the intercept evidence as I've mentioned, which I'll briefly outline. You recall the intercept from 16 July at 1358 hours. This is an intercept which is a four-part intercept which involves a duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade, Milorad Trbic, who was attempting to get fuel that has been requested by Mr. Popovic, and that's the intercept that talks about the 500 litres of D2 fuel. And he tells the duty officer that Mr. Popovic needs it. He then gets on the phone and talks to Mr. Basevic, the Technical Services officer of the Drina Corps Rear Services, and he tells him that he has to -- he conveys the message, 500 litres of D2 are urgently being asked for by Mr. Popovic or else the work he's doing will stop. He speaks to Pavle Golic, and he says: "Pop just called me, told me to contact you. 500 litres of D2 have to be sent to him immediately. Otherwise, his work will stop." And he says: "Yes, 500 litres or else his work will stop." He speaks to another unidentified participants and says: "A bus loaded with oil is to go to Pilica village." There's clear evidence in this case, Your Honours, that connect Mr. Popovic to those executions. You'll recall that there are additional intercepts where Mr. Popovic is referred to as being in the Zvornik area. There is the duty officer's notebook which indicates, also at 1400 hours, that a request for a bus with a full tank and 500 litres of D2, and that the duty officer and Golic have been informed of that. It's a prime example of how the security organ and the Security Administration is functioning within the normal command structures of both the brigade and the corps. You've seen the fuel dispatch order that's dated 16 July, which reads: "For Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic." And you've heard testimony that there was, in fact, fuel that was delivered near Pilica. You've seen the intercept at 2116 hours on 16 July, P01201, where Mr. Popovic reports to the Drina Corps Command, he speaks to Ljubo Rakic, actually: "Tell the general I've finished the job, I've finished the job, I've finished everything." And then on 17 July, at 1622, there's another intercept where Mr. Popovic speaks to his commander, General Krstic, and he says: "Hello, it's Popovic. Boss, everything is okay. That job is done." Further on in the intercept, he says: "That all gets an A, A, the grade is A. Everything is okay. That's it. Bye, and take care." Now, at paragraph 590, the Defence brief cites Krstic -- cites, I'm sorry, the Krstic Appeals judgement for the proposition that no reasonable trier of fact could have concluded that this was the only reasonable inference that could be drawn from the evidence; that is, that the job that he was doing concerned the burials and executions on the 16th and 17th of July. They cite the Krstic appeals judgement, and that's at paragraph 115 of that judgement. I would submit that the record before this Trial Chamber is a different one. It's different than the record that went before the Krstic Trial Chamber. You have here in this record eye-witness testimony placing Mr. Popovic and Mr. Beara at the Kula school, and that frames the context of this intercept. On the record before you, the only reasonable inference that you can draw from this intercept, in view of Mr. Popovic's presence at the school, is that this is exactly what he's doing, is he's reporting on the only job that he's doing in the area, and he's reporting on the successful completion of that operation. Your Honours, there is only one reason that explains Mr. Popovic's presence at any one of the execution sites in this case, let alone the several. He was there to see that the murder of the Muslim men and boys of Srebrenica was carried out efficiently, and he was there to see that it was carried out quietly. He was there to see it to its completion and to see to its concealment, and he was there pursuant to the orders of his commanders, to galvanise the resources needed to carry out this operation through the command structures of the VRS and especially of the Zvornik Brigade. His guilt as a member of the forcible transfer JCE, as charged under the indictment, is proven to no lesser extent, and based on the record of these proceedings, Your Honours, Mr. Popovic should be found guilty of each count under the indictment. There is no persuasive evidence in this record of any remorse from Mr. Popovic nor of any legitimate mitigation for his conduct, and I would ask you -- we ask that you take this into serious consideration in your judgement on the issue. I thank you for your indulgence, and, more importantly, I thank you for your patience and attention. And this concludes my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. I take it you are next, Mr. Mitchell. We are only five minutes away from the break. I suggest that we take the break and you start immediately after if that is convenient and agreeable to you. Okay, thank you. So we'll have a 25-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good morning, everyone. I'm going to respond briefly to some of the arguments raised by the Defence for Drago Nikolic in their final brief. First, I'd like to address some of their arguments about Drago Nikolic's contributions to the two joint criminal enterprises he's being charged with. Second, I'll address two discreet legal issues in relation to state policy to commit genocide and conspiracy to commit genocide. Finally, I'll address the Defence's submissions on mitigation. Before I start, I'd just like to say a few words about the Defence's final brief. This document contains a number of errors of law, of fact, and of analysis. It won't be possible to identify all of these errors today, but I would briefly like to highlight a couple up front, and I will address others in more detail as I go along. At paragraph 667 of their brief, the Defence state that: "Another important issue is the fact that Galic," referring to Mihajlo Galic, "was responsible for mobilisation matters, that there were many mobilisation issues which happened during the period of 13 to 15 July 1995, and that Galic denied being involved in any of them." This isn't a fair representation of Galic's testimony. At transcript page 10514, Galic confirmed that he actually met the new recruits on the morning of 15 July. Another example appears at paragraph 675 of the Defence brief, where they claim that three military experts, including Richard Butler, agreed with the suggestion that Dragan Obrenovic would have personally selected the officer who would have replaced Drago Nikolic at IKM on the night of 13th July. At transcript page 20448 to 20449, Mr. Butler said the exact opposite of what the Defence have quoted. Mr. Butler said: "I would have expected that Major Obrenovic would have verified that the position was filled. I don't believe that within the context of the operation staff that it would have been necessary for Major Obrenovic to hand pick the next duty officer." Another misstatement appears at paragraph 574, where the Defence state that Damjan Lazarevic testified that Drago Nikolic was not involved in the reburials. Again, this isn't a fair reflection of Lazarevic's testimony. At transcript pages 14507 to 14508, Lazarevic simply said that he didn't see Drago Nikolic during this period. I don't want to belabour this point with any more examples. We have no doubt that Your Honours will scrutinise the submissions of all parties in this case very carefully. I'd like to turn now to the Defence's arguments about the joint criminal enterprise to murder the men from Srebrenica, and the first argument I'd like to address is the argument that Drago Nikolic was not relieved from the IKM on the night of 13 July. It's uncontested that Drago Nikolic was the duty officer at the IKM during the day and the early evening of 13 July. The evidence has shown that at around 7.00 or 8.00 p.m., Drago Nikolic received a call from Vujadin Popovic, who told Nikolic to prepare for a large number of prisoners who were being brought to the Zvornik area to be shot. Later that night, Momir Nikolic personally told Drago Nikolic that those prisoners were going to be executed. Drago Nikolic called his commander and was authorised to leave the IKM and take some Zvornik Brigade military police, and the military police commander, Lieutenant Jasikovac, to organise the detention and the execution of those men. Mihajlo Galic testified that he replaced Drago Nikolic as the IKM duty officer that night, and the IKM log-book, which is Exhibit P347, confirms beyond any doubt that Drago Nikolic was replaced by Mihajlo Galic. We know that the first prisoners arrived at the Orahovac school that night, including PW-169, and we know that Zvornik Brigade military police were deployed to the school, including Stenoje Bircakovic, Dragoje Ivanovic, and PW-143. At transcript page 6532 to 6533, and 6611 to 6612, PW-143 testified that he actually saw Drago Nikolic at the Orahovac school that night. Drago Nikolic was the assistant commander for security. The arrival of these prisoners and the deployment of the MPs to guard them required his personal presence at the school that night. He had to be relieved, and he was relieved. Now, the Defence have argued that Drago Nikolic did not leave the IKM that night. They argue that the witnesses Mihajlo Galic, PW-168, PW-143, and Momir Nikolic were not credible. I don't intend to respond to this in any detail. These witnesses were reliable, they were consistent, and they were strongly corroborated. And I'd just like to direct Your Honours to paragraphs 2615 to 2646 for our detailed submissions about these witnesses. And the second point that I want to address is raised at paragraph 680 to 698 of the Defence's final brief, where they claim that there's evidence that the IKM log-book has been tampered with. Your Honours, I have the original book here, if you'd like to take another look at it. But very simply, this book is reliable, it's contemporaneous, there's absolutely no evidence that it's been tampered with, and there's no evidence whatsoever that Mihajlo Galic fabricated the key entry. The Defence's arguments about this book are also contradictory. At paragraph 688 and 690, they suggest that pages may have been removed from the book. On the other hand, at paragraph 694, they argue that it's suspicious that there are no pages missing from the book. You can't have it both ways. There is no credible basis for their arguments about the integrity of this book. Thirdly, Drago Nikolic relies on the evidence of Dragan Stojkic to support his claim that he remained at the IKM that night, but Stojkic's own testimony showed that he can't have been at the IKM on the night of 13 July, as he claimed. Stojkic was a member of Tactical Group 1 which went to Srebrenica and Zepa. At transcript pages 21971 to 21973, Stojkic testified that he stated sending Rijeka on the night of 11 July while he was en route to Zepa. According to him, he participated in fighting the next day near Zepa, which would have been 12 July, and the next day he returned to Zepa and went to the IKM. That was 13 July, according to him. It's clear that Stojkic's testimony and his timeline are two days out. Tactical Group 1 stayed at Rijeka on the night of 13 July and participated in one day of fighting in Zepa on 14 July. An example of that evidence came from Dragutinovic at transcript page 12591 to 12592. If Drago Nikolic stayed at Tactical Group 1, it had to have been on 13 July and he couldn't have been at the IKM as he claimed. At paragraph 654 of his brief, the Defence also suggests that Stojkic's testimony is corroborated by the fact that a tank company from Tactical Group 1 returned on the 13th of July. This is completely irrelevant. Stojkic was not a member of a tank company. Moreover, if Stojkic had returned on the 13th of July, he could not have participated in that one day of fighting in Zepa on the 14th. Your Honours, Stojkic was clearly mistaken about the dates when he was at the IKM, and his testimony cannot support the Defence's claim that Drago Nikolic remained at the IKM on 13 July. The totality of evidence on this point proves beyond any reasonable doubt that Drago Nikolic was relieved of duty at the IKM on the night of 13 July. Now, the Defence has also argued that Drago Nikolic thought that the men who were brought to Zvornik were going to be exchanged. This argument is completely implausible. First, the evidence has shown that Popovic and Momir Nikolic explicitly told Drago Nikolic on the night of 13 July that these men were going to be executed. Secondly, this looks nothing like an exchange. As outlined at paragraphs 2647 to 2666 of our final brief, there is no legitimate explanation for placing these prisoners in schools in the Zvornik area rather than the Batkovic camp. These prisoners were kept in appalling conditions. They had no food, no medical attention. They had insufficient water. Their personal belongings and their identification were stripped from them. And, most importantly, there were no lists made of the prisoners, and there was no one to exchange them for. Drago Nikolic was the assistant commander for security, and the evidence has shown that he had been involved in exchanges since at least 1993. The reference for that is Exhibit 3D -- 7D00454. Had Drago Nikolic genuinely thought that those prisoners at the Orahovac school were going to be exchanged, the first thing he would have asked when he went to the school was, Where are the list of the prisoners and who are we exchanging them for? This was no exchange, and Drago Nikolic knew full well that this was no exchange. The Defence have conceded that Drago Nikolic was at the Orahovac school twice on 14 July, and they also concede that he would probably incur some liability on that basis. However, at paragraph 71 of their brief, the Defence argue that Nikolic did not have any role in directing, supervising, or assisting the preparation or the organisation of the execution of the prisoners there. And Mr. Nikolic's role in coordinating the events at Orahovac is discussed a great length in our brief, but I would like to respond to this briefly and highlight the key parts of the evidence of his coordinating the events at the school and at the execution site. Dragoje Ivanovic testified that around 8.00 a.m. on the 14th of July, Drago Nikolic arrived at the school. I'd just like to read you a short section of Ivanovic's testimony on this point from transcript page 14544: "In the morning, around 8.00, the brigade chief Nikolic came, and shortly afterwards some 20 to 30 soldiers arrived as well. He told Jasikovac that we were free to go but that we should be ready and close by with the mini-bus. He told that the soldiers that arrived with him were there to take over the civilians." Ivanovic's testimony establishes clearly that Drago Nikolic was coordinating the change-over of security from the MPs who had arrived there the previous night to the soldiers who arrived there that morning. This necessarily means that he was coordinating and overseeing the detention of those prisoners. Now, just to be clear, it's Lieutenant Jasik ovac who gave the order to those MPs to stay around, but it's equally clear that Lieutenant Jasikovac was passing on Drago Nikolic's instructions to the MPs. This is a perfect example of how the relationship between Mr. Nikolic, Lieutenant Jasikovac, and the military police worked both by regulation and in practice. Later that morning, Drago Nikolic went to the Hotel Vidikovac with Milorad Bircakovic, and he met buses full of prisoners who had come from Bratunac. At transcript page 11054 to 11055, Milorad Bircakovic testified that Drago Nikolic told him to get on a bus and go to Orahovac. He's put the additional security in place that morning, and now he's coordinating the arrival of the additional prisoners. At around 11.00, Nikolic returned to the Orahovac school, and over the next few hours he was seen by numerous witnesses, including Milorad Bircakovic, at transcript 11022; PW-142 at transcript 6451 to 6452; PW-143, transcript 6536 to 6538; Stenoje Bircakovic, transcript 10748; Dragoje Ivanovic, transcript 14544 to 14548; Tanacko Tanic, transcript 10337; and PW-101 at transcript 7573 to 7534. PW-142 saw Drago Nikolic speaking with senior high-ranking officers at the school. Dragoje Ivanovic saw Drago Nikolic and Lieutenant Jasikovac speaking with a senior VRS officer. PW-143 also saw Nikolic speaking with a senior VRS officer who he testified was not from the Zvornik Brigade. Mr. Nikolic's meeting with Lieutenant Jasikovac and senior VRS officers at the school further established that he was there in a supervisory role. The evidence has also shown that Drago Nikolic and his deputy, Milorad Trbic, were at the Orahovac school after the transport and the execution of the prisoners had started. That evidence is outlined at paragraphs 2703 to 2716 of our brief. PW-101, in particular, saw Mr. Nikolic coordinating the transport of the prisoners from the school when he went there sometime after 8.30 p.m. that night. This was around the same time that Milorad Bircakovic testified that Drago Nikolic had returned to the Orahovac school just before dark. That's at transcript 11023. I'd also like to briefly touch on the role of the military police at Orahovac, which is summarised at paragraphs 2696 to 2702 of our final brief. Their involvement in the execution process is extremely significant because, through Lieutenant Jasikovac, their activities at the school were directed by Drago Nikolic. The military police guarded the prisoners, they helped blindfold the prisoners, they placed the prisoners on trucks that took them to the execution site. PW-142 testified that on at least one occasion, MPs actually escorted the prisoners to the execution site, and we also heard evidence from MP Milorad Bircakovic, who was Drago Nikolic's driver, that he escorted a number of these trucks to the water point which we know was the second execution site. And despite their claims to the contrary, these military police must have known that those prisoners were being executed. They even tried to cover up their involvement at Orahovac by doctoring the MP roster and removing the references to Orahovac on 14 July and the references to Rocevic on 15 July. The Trial Chamber has also heard credible evidence that Drago Nikolic was at the Orahovac execution site that day. PW-143 saw Drago Nikolic leave the Orahovac school and drive in the direction of the execution site. That's at transcript 6614. PW-101 saw Drago Nikolic at the execution site, overseeing the execution process with another senior VRS officer who matched the contemporaneous description of Mr. Popovic. I'd like to quickly read what PW-101 said about Drago Nikolic's role at the execution site: "He was there because the men who were escorting prisoners from the trucks, he was to direct them, because the other men who were there were executing people, firing at them, and that was their job, whereas Drago was with these others. He wasn't yelling at them or anything of that kind. He was simply directing them what to do." At one point during the day on 14 July, Drago Nikolic returned to the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, where he met with PW-102 and PW-108. As Your Honours have heard, Drago Nikolic told PW-102 that he had been executing prisoners at Orahovac. The executions -- or the evidence has shown that the executions continued long after dark. This evidence is outlined at paragraphs 743 to 750 of our brief. Milorad Bircakovic testified that he and Drago Nikolic drove past the execution site twice just after dark. The executions must have been ongoing at that time. Your Honours, there's a single compelling story that emerges from the testimony of these witnesses. Drago Nikolic coordinated the detention, the transport, and the execution of the prisoners at Orahovac, both at the school and at the execution site, and he made sure that those orders to kill the prisoners were carried out. I'd now like to address the Defence's submissions about the inferences that can be drawn from Drago Nikolic's meeting with Mr. Popovic and Mr. Beara on the morning of 14 July and his meeting with Mr. Beara outside the Petkovci school on the afternoon of 14 July. At paragraph 1173 of their final brief, the Defence have argued that Drago Nikolic merely learned of an imminent exchange of detainees at the meeting with Mr. Popovic and Mr. Beara on the morning of 14 July. And to put this meeting in context, as outlined in our brief and as summarised by Mr. Vanderpuye this morning, Mr. Beara and Mr. Popovic clearly knew about the murder operation at the time of this meeting, and they were both engaged in it. Drago Nikolic was their trusted colleague, and they needed his help. Even if we completely ignore the evidence that Drago Nikolic found out on the night of 13 July that the prisoners were going to be executed, there is no conceivable way that Mr. Popovic and Mr. Beara would have concealed this information from Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt you, but on the LiveNote the transcript has stopped; not on the main monitor, but since, I suppose -- shall we move without -- no, okay. Is there any objection from the Defence teams to proceed? No objection. We proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The events that happened after this meeting also show that the murder operation must have been discussed. The prisoners arrived from Bratunac that morning. The preparations for the executions at Orahovac were completed, the blindfolds were prepared, the trucks were obtained to transport the prisoners, and we know that the excavator was sent to Orahovac before noon that day. PW-104 also testified that Mr. Beara asked the Zvornik civilian authorities to assist in the burial of the prisoners who were going to be murdered. The 1st Battalion and the 6th Battalion also received information from the Zvornik Brigade Command that prisoners were going to arrive at the Kula school and the Petkovci school respectively. These prisoners were killed quickly and efficiently in less than three days. In all the surrounding circumstances, the purpose of that meeting on the morning of 14 July could only have been to coordinate the murder operation. The same conclusion applies to Drago Nikolic's meeting with Mr. Beara outside the Petkovci school that afternoon. This meeting happened, according to Marko Milosevic, between 4.00 and 5.00 p.m. This is after the executions at Orahovac had started and just hours before the prisoners at Petkovci were killed. It's completely unreasonable to think that Mr. Beara was hiding information about the murder operation from Drago Nikolic at this time. There can be no doubt that Drago Nikolic knew about the murder operation and was at the very heart of it. Your Honours, the Defence has made detailed submissions about Drago Nikolic's role in the detention and execution of prisoners who were held at the Kula school and the Rocevic school. I'm not going to respond to those arguments in detail. They're dealt with at length in our brief. But I would like to just direct Your Honours and the parties to the specific submissions in our brief. Paragraphs 2676 to 2684 outline Nikolic's involvement with the prisoners at Kula and the instructions he gave to Slavko Peric. The evidence has shown at the time he spoke with Slavko Peric, he knew that those prisoners were going to be killed. Paragraphs 2738 to 2762 outlines the evidence that the Zvornik Brigade could send and receive coded telegrams, that two coded telegrams were sent to the 2nd Battalion Command in the early morning of 15 July, ordering the formation of an execution squad, and that Drago Nikolic called the 2nd Battalion Command on the morning of 15 July to follow up on those telegrams and insist that executioners needed to be found. Finally, paragraphs 2770 to 2775 outline the evidence from PW-165 that Drago Nikolic went to the Rocevic school on 15 July with Milorad Trbic and issued instructions to the MPs who were there. Again, at the time Drago Nikolic was at the Rocevic school, he knew that the prisoners who were held there were going to be killed. The last point I'd like to address in relation to the joint criminal enterprise to murder the men from Srebrenica is the Defence's submissions at paragraphs 1295 to 1301 of their brief, that Drago Nikolic had nothing to do with the interrogation and execution of the four Branjevo Farm survivors. Now, as outlined at paragraphs 1057 to 1058 of our final trial brief, the evidence has clearly shown that these three Muslim men and one boy survived the mass executions at Branjevo Farm. These four survivors were captured, they were transported to the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, and they were interrogated by military police members, Nebojsa Jeremic and Cedo Jerovic [phoen]. And Nebojsa Jeremic testified that Drago Nikolic oversaw the work of the Crime Prevention Unit. That means that the interviews with those four survivors had to have taken place with Drago Nikolic's knowledge and his authorisation. Drago Nikolic also personally participated in this investigation by attending a line-up at which the -- at which the four survivors identified the two Zvornik Brigade soldiers who had assisted them. Nikolic also attended the interview of one of those Zvornik Brigade soldiers, and he signed the ruling against them for collaborating with the enemy. The evidence has shown that after Nikolic found out that these four prisoners had survived the Branjevo Farm executions, Nikolic spoke with his commander, Vinko Pandurevic, and the four prisoners disappeared shortly thereafter. Drago Nikolic oversaw every aspect of this investigation. There is no question that he was involved in the disappearance and the murder of those four victims. I'd like to turn now to the Defence's submissions about Mr. Nikolic's involvement in the forcible transfer of the Muslim populations of Srebrenica and Zepa. Mr. Nikolic has argued that he had no knowledge and no involvement in the forcible transfer of the Muslim population from Srebrenica. Your Honours, this argument is both factually and legally incorrect. The indictment makes it clear that the common purpose of that joint criminal enterprise was to force the Muslim populations out of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. The reference to the Muslim population clearly includes the men. Now, as we argued in our Rule 98 bis submissions, the language to "outside the control of the RS" which appears in paragraph 49 of the indictment, does not define the purpose and the goal of that joint criminal enterprise. Now, the evidence shows that most of the Bosnian Muslim population of Srebrenica and Zepa actually were removed to areas outside the RS, but the final destination of those people is not a material element of that crime. It's the act of forcing them out of the enclaves from an area where they were lawfully present, without grounds permissible under international law, that constitutes the criminal element of this offence. The indictment makes it clear that the men -- the Muslim men from Srebrenica are alleged to be the victims of forcible transfer. Paragraph 62 of the indictment alleges that the men who were separated from their families in Potocari were the victims of forcible transfer. Paragraph 63 of the indictment alleges that the men who surrendered along the road were the victims of forcible transfer. And paragraph 48(E) specifically states that the forcible transfer of the Muslim population included the forcible bussing of the men up to the Zvornik area where they were ultimately executed. The people who receive and detain these victims of forcible transfer at any point are as much a part of the plan to forcibly transfer these individuals as the people who attacked the Srebrenica enclave physically, the people who carried out the separations in Potocari, and the people who captured those Muslim men along the road. Mr. Nikolic participated in the coordination of the transport and the detention of those prisoners at a meeting with Mr. Beara and Mr. Popovic on the morning of 14 July. After that meeting, he went and met some of the buses which were transporting those prisoners, and he directed them to Orahovac. He also oversaw the detention of these prisoners once they had actually reached the schools in the Zvornik area. Drago Nikolic was a vital link in the chain which had forced those Muslim men out of the Srebrenica enclave or out of the enclaves and up to the Zvornik area. He clearly knew about and was involved in the forcible transfer joint criminal enterprise. I'd like to turn now briefly to two legal points which are raised in the Defence's brief. Firstly, the Defence have argued that the existence of a state policy to commit genocide is a necessary element of the crime. Quite simply, it's not. It's not contained in the Genocide Convention, it's not contained in the Statute of our Tribunal, and the Appeals Chamber in the Jelisic appeals judgement specifically states at paragraph 48 that the existence of a plan or policy is not a legal ingredient of the crime. In relation to conspiracy to commit genocide, the Defence has argued at paragraphs 141 to 187 of their final brief, and paragraphs 1596 to 1659, that even if there was a conspiracy to commit genocide, it was concluded sometime on the night of 11 July and Drago Nikolic could not subsequently join it. The conspiracy is clearly outlined at paragraph 34 of the indictment. It has the same duration and the same underlying facts as the joint criminal enterprise to murder the men from Srebrenica. Now, the law is clear that a person is liable for conspiracy to commit genocide at the moment they enter into an agreement with others to commit genocide, but that doesn't mean that the actual conspiracy stops at that point. As different people agreed to join that conspiracy on 12 July, on 13 July, on 14 July, on 15 July, that is the moment at which they are guilty of the crime to commit genocide. It's that act of agreement which their criminal liability attaches to. Your Honours, the moment when Drago Nikolic agreed to join the conspiracy is clear. On the night of 13 July, he received a call and was asked to join in the murder operation. Shortly afterwards, he called his commander and asked to be relieved from the IKM, and he was relieved from the IKM. The call to his commander and his relief from the IKM are conclusive proof that Drago Nikolic had agreed with others to commit genocide. The last point I'd like to address briefly are the Defence's submissions on mitigation. At paragraphs 1334 and 1336, for example, of the Defence's brief, they argue that Drago Nikolic's junior rank, the fact that he was following orders, and the fact that he was engulfed by these events diminishes his responsibility and his importance for sentencing purposes. These arguments should be given no weight whatsoever. Drago Nikolic was not obliged to commit these crimes. Drago Nikolic wasn't forced to follow any orders. He was not engulfed by events beyond his control. He had a choice. There's no doubt that it would have taken a lot of moral courage, but he could have chosen to say, No, and it was his legal and his moral obligation to say, No. Instead, he requested and he received authorisation to leave his post at the IKM and join in that genocidal plan, and every criminal act he participated in during the following days and weeks was by his choice. These are not the actions of a junior officer who was out of his depth or who was pressured into following orders. These are the actions of a man who knowingly and who intentionally committed the crimes with which he is charged in the indictment. And on that basis, we ask Your Honours to find him guilty of all the counts with which he is charged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitchell. Who is next; Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I am going to just move up to the podium and go next. Your Honours, Counsel, good morning. Firstly, I'm going to address certain issues in relation to the opportunistic killings and persecutions charged in the indictment as foreseeable consequences of the two joint criminal enterprises. The indictment sets out the relevant crime incidents at paragraphs 31 and 48, or paragraphs 37 and 83 charge that such crimes were foreseeable to the members of the murder JCE and the forcible removal JCE. I'm not going to rehearse the factual details which are covered in the final brief, starting at page 119 for Potocari, Bratunac, and the Kravica supermarket, and starting at page 224 for the Petkovci school. However, I will deal with specific factual allegations where those have been raised in the Defence briefs. As a preliminary matter, the Prosecution yesterday filed a corrigendum to the final brief which stated that certain opportunistic killings were no longer charged.
